claims.text: A neural-network interatomic potential can be trained for high-temperature multicomponent materials covering both solid and liquid states.
Replacing traditional EAM references with such a neural-network potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch associated with TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The proposed reference should be trained on a diverse set of high-temperature ab initio configurations spanning ordered solid and disordered liquid regimes.
A neural-network potential can be used as the reference potential in TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration.
The method applies to high-entropy alloys having typically at least five elements in near-equimolar proportions.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9–1.1 times the alloy melting temperature.
Neural-network potentials capture many-body interactions and subtle local coordination environments better than traditional EAM potentials.
Training on broad high-temperature ab initio data produces a more accurate energy landscape for both solid and liquid high-entropy alloys.
A more accurate solid-and-liquid energy landscape makes the configurations sampled by the reference potential better match those of the target ab initio system.
The neural-network reference will significantly reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to EAM.
The neural-network reference will yield free energies closer to direct ab initio benchmarks than EAM references do.
Elemental and binary calculations provide preliminary evidence for the predicted improvement.
The resulting free-energy differences may be within an approximately 10% error margin.
A DeepMD potential trained for binary HfC predicted melting behavior with no more than 10% deviation from experimental melting-temperature data.
Traditional EAM potentials inadequately sample the full configurational space of high-temperature ab initio liquids.
The approach should be robust for high-entropy alloys throughout the 0.9–1.1 Tm interval.
Compositions or atomic environments substantially outside the training domain may require adaptation or retraining.
The precise quantitative reduction in integration-path mismatch remains unknown pending direct benchmark studies.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement of roughly 10%, or performance no better than EAM against an ab initio benchmark, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted ~10% quantity is presented as an absolute free-energy error margin, whereas the falsification rule treats ~10% as a relative reduction in path mismatch. These are different metrics, so the stated threshold does not directly test the quantified prediction.

The design proposes comparing computed free energies with direct ab initio melting-temperature benchmarks; free energy and melting temperature are different observables unless an explicit free-energy-based melting criterion is defined.
